To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

anger, not guilt, predicts willingness for political action to address ingroup advantage, that anger is self-focused, and that guilt and anger about ingroup advantage predict the desire for systemic compensation, but anger, not guilt predicts willingness to act to achieve systemic compensation.
anger about ingroup advantage predicted the willingness to take action to bring about political change to reduce ingroup advantage, whereas guilt was unrelated to political action.

(1) non-Aboriginals’ anger and guilt about their ingroup advantage over Aborigines predict their willingness to engage in action to address this inequality, and (2) these two emotions are self-focused in that they are more strongly associated with appraising ingroup (rather than government) responsibility for the inequality than with appraising government responsibility.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how group-based emotions are associated with political action.
the role of guilt and anger in intergroup relations and their implications for political action.
the role of guilt and anger about group advantage in predicting the willingness for political action to reduce ingroup advantage.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

guilt is a more self-oriented and abstract emotion whereas anger is more group-oriented and specific emotion, which makes it a more powerful predictor of willingness for political action in the present context.
anger, but not guilt, is associated with willingness to act on behalf of the victimized outgroup.
anger and guilt are important in intergroup relations, but they have different implications for action.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the emotion of anger about ingroup advantage can be a powerful motivator for political action to reduce intergroup inequality.
guilt and anger about ingroup advantage are associated with willingness for political action to reduce the disadvantage of a structurally disadvantaged outgroup.
the willingness for political action is explained more by anger and guilt about ingroup advantage than by guilt about ingroup disadvantage.
The main takeaway from our work is that
anger and guilt about one’s group’s advantaged position are important predictors of the willingness to engage politically in the service of social justice.
anger and guilt are important predictors of political engagement.
guilt and anger about ingroup advantage are associated with the willingness to take political action to address ingroup advantage.
